papers.title: DeepWaveRL: Self-Supervised Full Waveform Inversion via Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Full Waveform Inversion (FWI) is a fundamental inverse problem in geophysics to estimate subsurface properties, such as velocity, from seismic measurements. Recently, self-supervised learning methods remove the need for ground-truth velocity maps during training by leveraging a forward operator to simulate seismic data from predictions and backpropagate the gradients of reconstruction loss through it. In this work, we consider a more challenging setting without accessing such gradients. To this end, we incorporate reinforcement learning into self-supervised FWI and propose a framework named DeepWaveRL. Specifically, we reformulate FWI as a policy learning problem, where the policy network predicts velocity maps as actions, and a forward operator is used solely for simulation. A global scalar reward is computed based on data misfit for each prediction and used to weight policy gradients. Thus, learning proceeds without accessing the gradients from the forward operator. Given the indirect and coarse supervision signals, we further identify key strategies to stabilize learning and mitigate the spatial credit assignment bottleneck. Experimental results show that, despite relying entirely on a single scalar reward, DeepWaveRL achieves competitive performance compared to supervised and self-supervised baselines. These findings suggest that our framework offers a flexible and complementary learning paradigm for the FWI research community.

papers.title: A Geometry-Informed Neural Operator surrogate of LISFLOOD-FP for rapid pluvial-fluvial flood forecasting: the case of Forl\`i, Italy
papers.abstract: Physically based two-dimensional hydraulic models are too slow for real-time inundation forecasting and large ensembles. We present a time-dependent geometry-informed neural operator (GINO) surrogate of LISFLOOD-FP for the municipality of Forl\`i (Italy), severely affected by the May 2023 Emilia-Romagna floods. The surrogate is designed for an operational setting in which only river stage gauges and rain gauges are available. A reproducible pipeline turns public regional observations into a physically based training set: each river inflow is driven by the first stage gauge downstream of it through a calibrated water-surface boundary condition, and rain enters as SCS-CN effective rainfall. The surrogate is an autoregressive GINO trained on 216 simulations of 24 observed events with scaled forcing. It predicts volume-conserving polygon-mean depths on an exposure-based Voronoi mesh of 659 nodes, with a 20 min step over 72 h. The surrogate is tested on 38 independent observed events that it never saw during training. On these events it reaches a critical success index (CSI) of 0.934 at 0.05m and 0.844 at 0.3 m, a depth RMSE of 0.008m and an $R^2$ of 0.984 for maximum-depth maps. On one NVIDIA A10G GPU a 72-h forecast takes 1.7 s instead of 55 s with LISFLOOD-FP, and a 50-member ensemble, computed in a single batched rollout, takes 6.2 s instead of about 46 min, which makes probabilistic flood forecasting practical. These results show that neural-operator surrogates can deliver accurate pluvial-fluvial flood forecasts driven by river stage for operational early warning.

papers.title: Community HydroAgent: Formalizing Forecaster Expertise into Skill-Orchestrated Flood Forecasting Workflows
papers.abstract: Operational flood forecasting depends on tacit forecaster expertise that is difficult to formalize, audit, and transfer. Although artificial intelligence methods have advanced flood prediction and model-error correction, few studies explicitly represent the tacit expert rules, review checkpoints, and workflow constraints that connect model outputs to operational warning decisions. Here, we propose Community HydroAgent for Flood Forecasting (CHA-Flood), a skill-orchestrated agent framework that embeds Large Language Models (LLMs) into a model-driven flood forecasting workflow, where each skill encodes explicit rules to bound LLM reasoning. We validated its effectiveness using five state-of-the-art LLMs in the South Yamhill River basin (USA). Prior judgment captures observed peak flow and flood volume within 5% tolerance in 10 and 11 out of 14 events, and 5-fold cross-validation over 129 events yields Pearson correlations of 0.62 and 0.84. Building on a high-baseline scheme library (average KGE 0.890), the guided scheme selection further improves KGE by 0.023-0.154. All five tested LLMs successfully execute the CHA-Flood workflow with comparable judgment accuracy (each spanning 40%-80% across cross-validation folds) but with substantial cost differences. Removing only the language-model narrowing lowers median KGE from 0.723-0.753 to 0.662 for all five LLMs, indicating that the gain comes from LLM reasoning rather than from the choice of LLM. CHA-Flood does not aim to replace human forecasters; instead, it translates their tacit expertise into an auditable and reproducible workflow. This skill-orchestrated paradigm demonstrates how explicit rule boundaries can guide LLM reasoning to complement physically based simulation in next-generation flood forecasting.

papers.title: Benchmark Study for Quantum Statevector Simulators for Scientific Computing
papers.abstract: Quantum circuit simulators are essential for quantum algorithm development, yet systematic runtime benchmarks comparing major frameworks across CPU and GPU backends are limited. We benchmark three open-source frameworks - Cirq (qsim), CUDA-Q, and Qiskit (Aer) - on statevector simulation of the 2D quantum acoustic wave equation, evolved via Trotterized Hamiltonian dynamics, for problem sizes from 7 to 29 qubits on a single Azure virtual machine. The evaluation spans four categories: CPU runtime versus qubit count, strong scalability on multi-core CPUs at 27 qubits, GPU runtime versus qubit count, and GPU-over-CPU speedup. Relative rankings shift from one category to the next. On CPU, Cirq is fastest up to 23 qubits (2.4x faster than Qiskit at 21 qubits), but Qiskit overtakes it at larger sizes and higher thread counts, sustaining 80% parallel efficiency at 16 threads. On GPU, CUDA-Q leads between 13 and 21 qubits, while Cirq becomes the fastest GPU backend at large problem sizes, achieving 1.5x and 2.3x speedups over CUDA-Q and Qiskit at 29 qubits. GPU-over-CPU speedup ratios should be interpreted alongside absolute GPU runtimes; CUDA-Q's 1500x at 21 qubits is largely driven by the limited scaling of its CPU backend (qpp), and the absolute GPU runtimes show that the three frameworks' GPU backends differ by less than these ratios alone suggest. These results indicate that no single framework dominates across configurations, and that backend selection for statevector simulation should be guided by both target hardware and problem size.

papers.title: Muography Simulations for Carbon Capture and Storage Monitoring
papers.abstract: Muography can monitor CO2 storage through reservoir density changes, but site-scale simulations are costly: reservoirs can be deep and borehole detectors are small. We address both with two approaches. First, a two-stage workflow splits the kilometer-scale simulation: a fast code transports muons through the overburden, and a general-purpose Monte Carlo code through the reservoir and detectors. Second, a geometric filter at the source keeps only muons whose direction and position let them reach the detectors, within a margin for multiple scattering, and a range cut removes those with too little energy. Both are available in the UCMuon simulation suite for muon generation, filtering and transport. At a deep (800-1000 m) and a shallow (65 m) CO2 storage site, each approach reduces the computing time about 700-fold, and the filtered simulation gives the same hit rate as a full one, as long as the margin exceeds the muons' sideways scattering drift.

papers.title: A spatial autocorrelation method for estimating Rayleigh-wave attenuation coefficients from microtremor array measurements
papers.abstract: The velocity and attenuation structures of near-surface soils play an important role in controlling earthquake ground motions. While numerous passive techniques have been developed for estimating velocity structure, practical methods for estimating attenuation from microtremor array measurements remain limited. We developed a spatial autocorrelation (SPAC) method for estimating Rayleigh-wave attenuation coefficients using an attenuation-aware formulation of the SPAC coefficient. A theoretical analysis of directional aliasing showed that attenuation estimation requires denser azimuthal sampling than conventional phase-velocity estimation, motivating the use of a regular heptagonal array. The method uses a two-stage procedure in which initial estimates of phase velocity and the attenuation coefficient are obtained using a first-order approximation and then refined by fitting the complex SPAC coefficient. Synthetic data analyses demonstrated that the proposed method can recover attenuation coefficients under ideal conditions and clarified how directional aliasing, record length and sensitivity to attenuation affect the estimates. Comparison with a beamforming-based method showed that the proposed method is less sensitive to wavefield directionality and can be applied at longer wavelengths relative to the array size. The method was further validated using microtremor-like waveforms generated by independent P--SV wave-propagation simulations. Finally, a preliminary application to field microtremor records yielded attenuation coefficients that were broadly consistent across array sizes and with values expected from existing empirical attenuation relationships. These results demonstrate the applicability of the proposed method to passive estimation of Rayleigh-wave attenuation.

papers.title: Original Insights Into Rock Slope Damage Processes Until Collapse From Passive Seismic Monitoring
papers.abstract: We conducted passive seismic monitoring of the unstable La Praz rock slope (approximately 14,000 m${}^3$) in the French Alps over a period of more than 10 years. During the six months preceding collapse, we observed a pronounced 24% decrease in the slope's fundamental resonance frequency ((f\_0)), indicating a reduction in the overall stiffness of the rock mass. Joint analysis of (f\_0) variations and slope deformation revealed alternating phases dominated by sudden brittle damage and more ductile behavior, potentially involving sliding. Seismic monitoring identified damage processes that were either ambiguous or undetectable through surface deformation measurements alone, while also highlighting critical periods of intensified damage. Although some of these periods coincided with identifiable external triggers, such as intense rainfall events, others could not be clearly linked to external forcing. These findings demonstrate the potential of passive seismic monitoring to provide insights into the internal structural condition of unstable rock slopes at depth. Combining surface deformation measurements with seismic tracking of rock mass stiffness could therefore improve the identification and characterization of active slopes undergoing progressive damage, contributing to the development of more effective slope monitoring systems.

papers.title: Characterizing landslide dynamics from time-lapse time domain induced polarization and ground-based imaging: a case study of the MontGombert landslide (French, Alps)
papers.abstract: Electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) is widely used to investigate landslide morphology and dynamics. Landslide behavior is strongly influenced by clay content, pore pressure, and the spatial distribution of permeability. However, conventional direct current (DC) resistivity methods have limited capacity to characterize permeability, as materials with low electrical resistivity may exhibit either high or low permeability depending on their clay content and the relative contributions of surface and electrolytic conduction. Induced polarization (IP) offers a valuable complementary approach for investigating the petrophysical properties of geological materials. Despite its potential, IP has been rarely applied to landslide studies and has not yet been widely used for landslide monitoring. This study investigates the added value of IP measurements alongside conventional DC resistivity for landslide characterization and monitoring. Three time-domain induced polarization (TDIP) surveys were conducted at different time steps on an active landslide in the French Alps. Time-lapse inversions of resistivity and chargeability were performed, and spectral IP parameters were derived using Debye decomposition. The results were then compared with surface displacement estimates obtained from optical image processing. The findings demonstrate that TDIP is particularly valuable for delineating unstable volumes within the landslide. The geophysical results show strong agreement with independent measurements from piezometers and inclinometers. Furthermore, applying an empirical relationship between IP parameters and permeability enables the spatial distribution of permeability within the landslide to be estimated, as well as its seasonal variations. Overall, this study highlights the potential of combining IP and DC resistivity measurements to improve the characterization of landslide properties and support the monitoring of their temporal evolution.

papers.title: Mapping rockfall hazard and detecting precursory damage in rock slopes with passive seismic: Lessons from the La Praz case-study
papers.abstract: Repeated passive seismic surveys were conducted over more than a decade on the unstable La Praz rock slope in Savoie, France, which involved an estimated rock volume of approximately 13,000--15,000 m${}^3$. The final survey took place two months before the complete collapse of the slope in August 2023. The amplitude of the Horizontal-to-Vertical Spectral Ratio at the peak frequency (*aHVSR(fp)*) was used to distinguish stable and unstable areas and identify fractures associated with significant mechanical decoupling. Rock compartments were also classified according to their rockfall hazard. The compartments most susceptible to failure exhibited the highest *aHVSR(fp)* values, ranging from 26 to 157, compared with values of 7.5--19 in intermediate-hazard areas and 2.7 in the adjacent stable rock mass. The main HVSR peak frequency (*fp*) exhibited distinct decreases of 15%, 14%, and 11% in three unstable rock compartments before the collapse. These reductions substantially exceeded the range of environmentally induced resonance-frequency fluctuations observed at the site and commonly reported in the literature as a limitation of this method. The frequency decreases were interpreted as indicators of progressive damage extending into the rock slope. Notably, these changes were detected exclusively in the three compartments identified as the most susceptible to failure, which also exhibited the highest *aHVSR(fp)* values. This study demonstrates, for the first time, the potential of passive seismic monitoring to reveal progressive in-depth damage within a complex, heterogeneous, and highly fractured rock slope. The findings highlight the value of combining HVSR amplitude and peak-frequency variations to characterize unstable rock compartments and identify potential precursors to catastrophic slope failure.

papers.title: Seismic study of soda straws exposed to nearby blasting vibrations
papers.abstract: This study aims to protect an exceptional population of soda straw stalactites from vibrations generated by nearby rock blasting activities. The Choranche Cave, located in the Vercors region of France, hosts thousands of remarkably slender soda straws, reaching several meters in length while measuring approximately 0.5 cm in diameter. These speleothems are particularly susceptible to vibrations because of their structural fragility and potential for dynamic amplification. Our analyses revealed that their fundamental natural frequencies fall within the frequency range of nearby blasting-induced vibrations, typically spanning tens to hundreds of hertz. To assess the effects of blasting, we combined in situ vibration measurements, laboratory-based material characterization, and dynamic two-dimensional finite element simulations to estimate the loads experienced by the soda straw population. The results indicate that resonance can amplify the induced loads by a factor of five. Consequently, shorter soda straws (0.1--1 m) were found to be more vulnerable to blasting-induced vibrations than longer speleothems (>1 m), despite the greater weight and inertial forces associated with the latter. Based on simulations of several blasting tests, we established an allowable peak particle velocity (PPV) threshold of 2.4 mm/s within the cave. Subsequent blasting operations were conducted in compliance with this limit, successfully protecting the soda straw population from damage. We also investigated the dynamic response of soda straws to regional earthquakes. papers.title: Environmental seismology: What can we learn on earth surface processes with ambient noise?
papers.abstract: Environmental seismology investigates mechanical vibrations generated by external processes or influenced by phenomena originating outside the solid Earth. It encompasses interactions between the solid Earth and other environmental systems, including the cryosphere, hydrosphere, and anthroposphere, as well as the specific sources of seismic vibrations associated with these systems. This field also examines how environmental factors, such as temperature fluctuations and hydrological variations, affect seismic wave propagation. Recent advances in data-processing techniques, combined with increased computational capabilities and the growing density of seismic sensor networks, have enabled novel observations and contributed to the emergence of environmental seismology as a distinct research field. This article reviews how subtle changes in the Earth's subsurface can be detected and interpreted through variations in seismic wave propagation induced by external environmental processes, with applications to geomechanics, hydrology, and natural hazard assessment. In particular, we demonstrate how ambient seismic noise can be used to monitor: (1) thermal variations in the subsurface, within buildings, and in rock columns; (2) the temporal and spatial evolution of groundwater levels; and (3) changes in the rigidity of the material forming a landslide, with particular emphasis on the reduction in rigidity that may precede slope failure.

papers.title: Damage Assessment of Supporting Pillars in an Underground Cave Using Joint Inversion of Electrical Resistivity and P-wave Velocity, Burgundy (France)
papers.abstract: This study presents an integrated approach combining seismic refraction tomography and electrical resistivity tomography to evaluate the structural integrity of supporting pillars in an underground cave in Burgundy, France. A three-phase petrophysical joint inversion (P-JIv) was performed using a finite-element model on an unstructured triangular mesh. Compared with independent inversions, the joint inversion improved spatial resolution and enhanced the consistency between the two geophysical methods. The results revealed distinct zones of electrical resistivity and P-wave velocity, reflecting variations in rock fracturing and weathering. The geophysical interpretations showed strong agreement with visual inspections and borehole logs. Furthermore, rock porosity and water content were estimated from the P-JIv results. Finally, an automated clustering procedure was used to establish a proxy indicator of pillar integrity, enabling the prioritization of cave reinforcement measures.
